item.title: China opens exhibition hall on language preservation, diversity
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
A visitor listens to dialects of various regions in Hunan at the Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 24, 2026. A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays. The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, located in the Hunan Museum, brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China, covering Chinese dialects, ethnic minority languages and related cultural traditions. (Xinhua/Xue Yuge) CHANGSHA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays. The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, located in the Hunan Museum, brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China, covering Chinese dialects, ethnic minority languages and related cultural traditions. More than 30 language-related cultural relics are also on display. The exhibition features original sound recordings representing 10 major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan, Uygur and Zhuang, said Chen Xuliang, deputy Party secretary of the Hunan Museum. Visitors can listen to regional dialects, folk songs and field recordings of some endangered languages, while interactive installations allow them to explore the development and diversity of languages across China, Chen added. The exhibition draws on materials collected through a national language preservation project launched in 2015 to document and preserve the country's diverse languages and dialects. It is the world's largest project of its kind, according to experts. An alliance was also launched on Monday, bringing together universities and research institutions to promote the use of language technologies in areas including education, scientific research and cultural preservation. ■ People visit the Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 24, 2026. item.title: U.S. military expansion in LatAm an "escalation of imperialism," says Brazilian analyst
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Washington's recent expansion of ground military operations in Colombia, Guatemala, Honduras and other Latin American countries represents an "escalation of imperialism" in the region, a Brazilian political observer has warned. Noting that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced the expansion earlier this month during his visit to Panama, Jose Luiz Niemeyer, an international relations professor at Brazil's Ibmec university, said the move marks a qualitative leap in Washington's interventionist policy, extending to ground operations the same approach it has used to strike boats in the Caribbean and Pacific. "It is an extremely concerning move and, unfortunately, is in keeping with the U.S. historical approach to our region," Niemeyer said in an interview with Xinhua. The United States is using the fight against drug trafficking not only to justify expanding its military presence, but also to impose "its security agenda without any regard for the sovereignty of Latin American countries," he said. "The attacks on vessels in the Caribbean and the Pacific were already a unilateral action with serious human rights violations, resulting in more than 200 deaths and little presented evidence. Now, by applying that same logic to ground operations in countries like Colombia, Ecuador and Guatemala, the United States is creating a highly dangerous precedent for direct interventions in our territory," he said. Niemeyer questioned Washington's narrative about striking agreements with allied countries, saying they ignore popular will and national laws. "What we are seeing is pressure from Washington on governments that are mostly ideologically aligned or in a position of political and economic vulnerability," he added. From the Monroe Doctrine to the Roosevelt Corollary to the recent "Donroe Doctrine," Latin American countries "are faced with the same logic of domination that reinvents itself throughout the centuries," Niemeyer said, describing the latter two as extension and revival of the Monroe Doctrine as Washington's guiding policy for the Western Hemisphere. By reviving that rhetoric with a play on the name of U.S. President Donald Trump, Washington "is saying out loud that the United States feels entitled to intervene wherever it wants in the region to 'defend its hemisphere,'" he said. "What concerns me is that this rhetoric is being accompanied by concrete actions, with training, intelligence gathering and joint operations," he said. "In the long term, this creates a military dependency that makes us hostages to Washington's volatile and aggressive foreign policy." Recalling the history of U.S. military intervention in the region, which is "full of troubling examples," the expert urged Latin American countries to stay alert. "The history of our region is full of examples of what happens when the United States decides to 'help' us with its armed forces: dictatorships, human rights violations, dirty wars and stunted development. Brazil, with its tradition of non-intervention, must raise its voice against this escalation that threatens the entire continent," he said.■

item.title: Opinion: What 9.39 seconds says about human ingenuity
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- At the second World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing on Saturday, China's Tien Kung Ultra humanoid robot clocked 9.39 seconds at the finish line, shattering the 9.58-second men's 100-meter world record set by Jamaican sprinter Usain Bolt 17 years ago. The comparison is irresistible, though the two feats are hardly equivalent: Bolt shows how fast the human body can run; the robot shows how far human ingenuity can go. At the current stage of humanoid robot development, running remains a formidable challenge. The robot must generate force, absorb repeated impacts and maintain dynamic balance while coordinating multiple joints simultaneously. Speed tests every technical limit: the faster the machine moves, the less time it has to recover from a mistake. That makes the pace of improvement remarkable. At last year's Games, Tien Kung Ultra took 21.5 seconds over the same distance. One year later, it had more than halved that time. Progress on that scale rarely comes from a single breakthrough. Over the past year, engineers upgraded the robot's joints, refined its structure and reworked its control algorithms for high-speed running. They have also improved its navigation, allowing it to hold its course at speed without relying on track markings. Breaking the human record, however, is never the ultimate goal of engineering. Every improvement reveals the next weakness. Even Saturday's 9.39-second run pointed to the next challenge: the robot had a slower start, although its higher top speed allowed it to pull ahead later in the race. Competition helps accelerate that process. It provides clear targets, common benchmarks and visible results. Once one team raises the bar, everyone else has a new standard to meet -- and proof that a higher level of performance is attainable. Ultimately, the goal of humanoid robot innovation is not simply to make robots move like humans, but to enable them to work alongside people and take on useful tasks in the real world. A factory robot does not need to win a sprint, nor does a service robot need a medal. But every gain in speed, stability and precision on the competition floor can bring robots one step closer to becoming genuinely useful beyond it. That is what gives 9.39 seconds significance beyond the stopwatch. The speed record captures how far the machine has come in a year; behind it are countless human decisions, experiments and refinements that made that progress possible. The next test will be how far those advances can go beyond the track.■

item.title: China, India to hold 25th round of talks on boundary question in Beijing
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China and India will hold the 25th round of talks between the two countries' special representatives on the boundary question in Beijing on Aug. 25, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson announced on Monday. As agreed between the two sides, Wang Yi, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs and China's Special Representative on the Boundary Question between China and India, will co-chair the talks with India's Special Representative and National Security Advisor Ajit Doval, said the spokesperson. ■

item.title: China issues multiple alerts for rainstorms, typhoons
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-24
BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) on Monday issued blue alerts for typhoons and severe convective weather and a yellow alert for rainstorms, with multiple typhoons forecast to bring heavy rainfall and strong winds to parts of the country. The China Meteorological Administration also raised its emergency response for major meteorological disasters from Level IV to Level III around Monday noon. Heavy rainfall is expected in parts of Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan from Monday to Wednesday, according to the NMC. Strong winds are also forecast over the Beibu Gulf, the Taiwan Strait and the East China Sea, as well as their coastal areas. Some areas of Liaoning and Jilin will see heavy rainfall on Monday, while a significant rain spell is expected to sweep eastward through the eastern part of northwest China, north China and northeast China from Tuesday, accompanied by severe convective weather, the NMC said. Typhoon Narra, the 19th typhoon of the year, was located at 4 p.m. Monday in waters about 260 kilometers southwest of Beihai City in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with maximum winds of 23 meters per second near its center. It is expected to track eastward from Monday night and then travel northward at a speed of 5 to 10 kilometers per hour, gradually approaching the coastal areas from Guangxi to the western Leizhou Peninsula in Guangdong Province, according to the NMC. China's National Development and Reform Commission has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.37 million U.S. dollars) in the central budget to support emergency recovery in Guangxi, where Typhoon Narra has already brought severe rainfall and floods. The fund will focus on restoring damaged roads, water infrastructure, schools and hospitals to help resume normal production and daily life as soon as possible, according to the commission. Typhoon Gaenari, the 20th typhoon of the year, made landfall along the coast of Quanzhou in east China's Fujian Province at around 12:30 p.m. on Monday, the local meteorological observatory said. Meanwhile, the NMC said Typhoon Saudel, this year's 18th typhoon, is expected to enter the East China Sea on Wednesday and gradually approach the coastal areas of east China. The NMC has advised local governments to take precautionary measures. China has a four-tier color-coded weather warning system, with red representing the most severe, followed by orange, yellow and blue. ■

item.title: China's tech city inspires youth discussions on Asia-Pacific's green future
item.description:
Published: 2026-08-23
Guests visit the Chunhui Substation in downtown Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Aug. 21, 2026.(Xinhua) SHENZHEN, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Young experts and scholars from the Asia-Pacific region gathered in Shenzhen, a world-leading tech hub in south China's Guangdong Province, to explore how the green energy transition could shape the region's future and their role in this endeavor. Themed "Asia-Pacific Youth Gathering: Building a Shared Future Through Energy," the event on Friday brought together over 60 experts, scholars and journalists from 13 countries and regions for dialogue and discussion panels. "Building a clean, secure and efficient energy system constitutes a vital cornerstone for the common prosperity of the Asia-Pacific," said Yu Guanyi, head of the think tank office of the APEC Sustainable Energy Center, at the opening ceremony of the event. Noting the importance of young voices in the green transition, Leo Barry, an Australian master's student at the Yenching Academy of Peking University, said that encouraging more young people to take part in such professional discussions is crucial to inspiring them to make real contributions to delivering a cleaner, greener and more prosperous future. Young representatives also visited China's first zero-carbon interactive substation, the 110-kV Chunhui Substation in downtown Shenzhen, to learn how green energy can deliver dependable power to fuel the metropolis' bustling industrial and commercial activities. With Shenzhen set to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in November, delegates paid extra attention to green-energy cooperation among countries in the region. The power network in the Asia-Pacific still faces common challenges such as accessibility and mismatches in resource and demand, which make energy cooperation within the region even more important, said Chhoeun Raksmey of Cambodia's Ministry of Industry, Science, Technology and Innovation. In response, Yang Bo, a project commercial specialist at China Southern Power Grid Co., Ltd., shared his insights. He has been involved in China's first 500-kV cross-border alternating-current power link in Laos, which came into operation in April. Earlier this month, hydropower from northern Laos reached the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area for the first time via the link, and is expected to reach a total transmission volume of approximately 600 million kWh by the end of October. "This bilateral power cooperation program allows Laos to translate its resource endowments into tangible economic gains for local communities, strengthening its role as a regional clean energy hub," Yang told Xinhua. Laos' green power arriving in Shenzhen comes as China deepens its green transition cooperation with regional partners. Under frameworks including the Belt and Road Initiative and the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation mechanism, China has actively participated in cross-border construction of clean energy projects in wind, solar, hydropower and energy storage, propelling the region's green development. Such cooperation also introduces leading photovoltaic technology, power-grid equipment, intelligent dispatching systems and energy-management solutions, helping advance power supply reliability and energy efficiency, said Chisa Jermwarayukorn, secretary-general of the Asia-Pacific Think Tank. She added that this approach will enable countries in the region to stay more closely connected and become long-term partners. "As neighbors with different resources, it's time for us to share our advantages, enhance bilateral and multilateral cooperation, and bring more tangible projects to the Asia-Pacific region, so as to achieve a green and sustainable future together," stressed Chhoeun Raksmey. ■
